parts.title: The green jacket
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
When I was fourteen, I hated the idea of wearing clothes that had belonged to someone else. My cousin Kayode loved charity shops, and every time he visited, he tried to take me to one. I always found an excuse. I thought the clothes would smell strange and look old-fashioned, and I was worried that my friends would laugh at me.

One rainy Saturday, however, there was nothing else to do, so I finally agreed to go with him. The shop was bigger than I had expected, and it was quiet and warm. Kayode went straight to the back, but I stayed near the door, looking at a rack of coats. Then I saw a green jacket with a soft collar and brass buttons. It was in perfect condition, and it only cost eight pounds. I tried it on, and the sleeves fitted exactly.

I wore the jacket to school on Monday, and I was very nervous. To my surprise, three people asked me where I had bought it. One girl wanted to know if the shop had more like it. I felt proud, and I realised that nobody could tell the jacket was second-hand. Since then, I have found shirts, bags and even a pair of leather boots in charity shops. I still enjoy walking round them slowly and looking for something that nobody else has. Kayode says he knew I would change my mind, but he was too polite to say so at the time.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer avoid charity shops at first?
options: She was afraid of what her friends would think.
She thought the prices were too high.
She did not enjoy shopping with her cousin.
questions.explanation: She was worried that her friends would laugh at her, and she expected the clothes to look old-fashioned.

questions.prompt: What made her go to the shop on that Saturday?
options: She wanted to buy a coat.
There was nothing else to do.
questions.explanation: It rained and there was nothing else to do, so she agreed to go.

questions.prompt: What did she like about the jacket?
options: It was a gift from her cousin.
Its colour matched her school uniform.
It was cheap and fitted her well.
questions.explanation: It cost only eight pounds and the sleeves fitted exactly.

questions.prompt: How did people react when she wore it to school?
options: They asked where she got it.
questions.explanation: Three people asked where she had bought it, and one girl wanted more shops like it.

questions.prompt: What does the writer say about Kayode at the end?
options: He was right about her but did not say it.
He now shops in different places.
He felt sorry about the idea.
questions.explanation: Kayode knew she would change her mind but was too polite to say so.

parts.title: A year without new clothes
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
Last January, Mia from Kelby made a promise: she would not buy any new clothes for a whole year. She had noticed that her wardrobe was full, but she still felt that she had nothing to wear. [1] She hoped the challenge would show her how much she really needed.

The first few months were not easy. Whenever her friends went to the shopping centre, she felt left out. [2] Instead, she took a bag and went to the market to look for second-hand pieces, or she borrowed clothes from her older sister.

By summer, Mia was enjoying the challenge. She learned to sew on missing buttons and to turn old jeans into shorts. [3] People she did not know began to follow her, and many of them sent her their own ideas for mending clothes.

At the end of the year, Mia counted what she had saved. [4] She says that the biggest surprise was not the money but the way she felt. She no longer looked at adverts and thought she needed everything.

Will she go back to her old habits? [5] "I want to buy fewer things and keep them for longer," she says.
sentences: It was more than four hundred pounds.
She also started to write about her projects online.
So she decided to try something different.
She did not want to spend her money on things she would wear only once.
Mia is sure that she will not.
A few of her friends also began to buy second-hand things.

gaps.explanation: "So she decided to try something different" follows her problem of having a full wardrobe but nothing to wear.
"Instead" follows the sentence about not buying at the shopping centre; sentence D explains why she avoided shops.
She learned to sew and mend, and then began to write about her projects online; the next sentences say that people followed her.
"It was more than four hundred pounds" answers what she counted, and the next sentence continues with the money.
The question "Will she go back to her old habits?" is answered by "Mia is sure that she will not."

parts.title: Dressing for the weather
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Choosing the right clothes can make a big [1] to how you feel on a cold day. Experts say that it is better to wear several thin layers [2] one thick coat, because you can take a layer off if you get too warm. Wool and cotton are good [3] for the bottom layer, as they keep your skin dry. Do not forget your hands and head: you lose a lot of heat [4] them. When it rains, a coat with a hood is more useful than an umbrella, especially if it is windy, [5] an umbrella is difficult to hold. Finally, it is worth spending a little more on warm socks, because cold feet can quickly [6] you unhappy.

questions.prompt: Gap 1
questions.explanation: You say that something "makes a difference" to how you feel.

questions.prompt: Gap 2
questions.explanation: "Instead of" means one choice replaces the other: thin layers instead of one thick coat.

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: "Good choices" means good things to choose; the other words do not fit with "for the bottom layer".

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: Heat escapes "through" the head and hands.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: "Because" gives the reason why an umbrella is difficult to hold when it is windy.

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: The structure is "make someone + adjective": make you unhappy.

parts.title: A message about shopping
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage:
Dear Tom,
I am writing to tell you about my shopping trip. I went to the new shopping centre [1] Saturday with my sister. We spent most [2] the afternoon looking for a dress for her birthday party, and in the end she chose the first one [3] had tried on! The shop was very busy, so we had to wait [4] a long time to pay. I also bought a pair of boots [5] I really love, but they cost more than I had planned. In future, I am going [6] buy my clothes at the market.
Lia

gaps.explanation: We use "on" with a day of the week: on Saturday.
"Most of the afternoon" is the fixed pattern: most of + noun phrase.
The relative clause needs a subject: the first one she had tried on.
We say "wait for a long time" for the length of the wait.
A relative pronoun links "boots" with the clause: boots that I really love.
The structure for plans is "be going to" + base verb.

turns.text: Good morning, everyone. I'm Bronwyn, and I'm in charge of this year's fashion show at Rowan School. The show takes place on Friday evening, and it starts at seven o'clock. parts.title: An interview with a costume maker
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Ottoline, you make costumes for the theatre. How did you start?

turns.speaker: ottoline
turns.text: I wanted to be an actress, but I was terrible on stage. A teacher saw me sewing costumes for the school play and said I should do that instead. She was right.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the first thing you do with a new play?

turns.speaker: ottoline
turns.text: I read the script twice and make notes about each character. Is she rich or poor? Is she shy? The clothes have to tell the audience that before she says a word.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Do you buy new cloth for every costume?

turns.speaker: ottoline
turns.text: Hardly ever. Theatres have little money, so I look for old clothes in charity shops and change them. A plain dress can look completely different with new sleeves and some paint.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the most difficult part of the job?

turns.speaker: ottoline
turns.text: Time. I always have to work very quickly. During a show I only have a few minutes to help an actor change. Last month someone's zip broke just before he went on stage, and I fixed it with safety pins in thirty seconds.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Do actors ever complain about their costumes?

turns.speaker: ottoline
turns.text: Sometimes. They tell me a hat is too heavy or a shoe pinches. I listen, because if an actor feels uncomfortable, the audience can see it.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What advice would you give to a young person who wants to do your job?

turns.speaker: ottoline
turns.text: Learn to sew properly, but also watch people. Look at how they dress on the bus or in the park. The best ideas come from real life, not from books.
